Item 7.01 - Regulation FD Disclosure
Officers of Elevance Health, Inc. (the “Company”) expect to speak with investors and analysts this week. During these meetings, Company officers will reaffirm the Company’s shareholders’ earnings guidance for full year 2026 to be at least $22.00 per diluted share, including approximately $7.00 per diluted share of net unfavorable items. Excluding these items, the Company continues to expect adjusted shareholders’ earnings to be at least $29.00 per diluted share. This does not include any other adjustment items beyond those reported in the Company's third quarter 2026 earnings.
During these meetings, Company officers will also reaffirm full year 2026 benefit expense ratio guidance of 90.2% plus or minus 50 basis points.
None of the information furnished in Item 7.01 hereto shall be deemed to be “filed” for purposes of Section 18 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended. Unless expressly set forth by specific reference in such filings, none of the information furnished in this report shall be incorporated by reference in any filing under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, whether made before or after the date hereof and regardless of any general incorporation language in such filings.

COSTCO WHOLESALE CORPORATION DECLARES $30 SPECIAL CASH DIVIDEND AND REAUTHORIZES STOCK REPURCHASE PROGRAM
ISSAQUAH, Wash., November 10, 2026 - Costco Wholesale Corporation (“Costco” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: COST) today announced that its Board of Directors has declared a special cash dividend of $30 per share on Costco common stock. It is payable December 4, 2026, to shareholders of record as of the close of business on November 24, 2026. The total amount of the payment will be approximately $13.3 billion.
The Company also announced that the Board has reauthorized a common-stock repurchase program of up to $4 billion. This program will expire in November 2030 and replaces the current $4 billion program (adopted in 2023 and scheduled to expire January 2027), under which $3.1 billion had been purchased.
Costco currently operates 945 warehouses, including 653 in the United States and Puerto Rico, 115 in Canada, 43 in Mexico, 37 in Japan, 29 in the United Kingdom, 20 in Korea, 15 in Australia, 14 in Taiwan, seven in China, five in Spain, three in France, two in Sweden, and one each in Iceland, and New Zealand. Costco also operates e-commerce sites in the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Mexico, Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Australia, and China.

The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy 
 Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman 
At the C. Peter McColough Series on International Economics Council on Foreign Relations, Washington, D.C. 
 Share 
 Watch Live 
Good afternoon. It is a pleasure to join you today at the Council on Foreign Relations to discuss my outlook for the U.S. economy.1 
Economic growth has gained momentum this year, driven by robust investment demand and solid consumer spending, and the labor market now appears to have stabilized. These outcomes suggest that the policy rate cuts toward the end of last year helped to address some labor market weakness. We are experiencing rapid technological change and ongoing geopolitical tensions, while inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening. Despite these challenges, increased investment in and use of artificial intelligence (AI), or super intelligence, are boosting economic growth and productivity and American families appear to be resilient. 
The Federal Reserve's monetary policy goals are to achieve maximum employment and price stability. While the labor market has improved more than I expected this year, our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed. Therefore, bringing inflation down remains a priority. I am also monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices, and how they influence the risks to achieving our mandates. Consistent with my views following our September FOMC meeting, I continue to focus on interpreting the underlying trends in the economy and the evolution of financial conditions.2 
In my remarks today, I will review our most recent FOMC policy meeting and discuss current economic conditions and my near-term outlook for the economy. I will then turn to recent developments in energy markets and the AI buildout and will conclude with my thoughts on the appropriate path of monetary policy. 
Update on the Most Recent FOMC Meeting
At last month's FOMC meeting, I joined my colleagues to support holding the federal funds rate target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent. This approach was consistent with my view that further changes in the policy rate should wait until we had a better understanding of how conditions would evolve and how the recent rate increase would influence the underlying trends in the economy. Maintaining the policy stance at the October meeting allowed us to assess the incoming data. While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated. It is also important to gain greater clarity on the effect of recent market volatility on financial conditions. 
Economic and Financial Conditions
U.S. economic growth has stepped up this year. After rising a solid 2.4 percent during the first half of the year, real gross domestic product (GDP) likely increased at an even stronger pace of more than 3 percent in the third quarter, well above last year's 2 percent pace.3 Economic growth has been supported by robust increases in AI-related capital expenditures and solid consumer spending. However, some interest-rate-sensitive sectors like residential investment have declined, and the recent rise in mortgage rates appears to be dragging home construction and sales down further. Consumer spending has strengthened this year, despite softness in real incomes and declining sentiment, which are partly due to higher energy prices. 
Labor Market Conditions
Labor market conditions look to have improved since last year. Over the course of this year, the unemployment rate has edged down to 4.1 percent in October, remaining close to my estimate of its natural rate. Job gains have been above last year's anemic pace, averaging about 80,000 per month through October, and have broadened across industries beyond health care and social assistance. 
The labor market continues to show low dynamism, with low-hiring and low-firing conditions as we sometimes see in a late-cycle expansion. The job-finding rate has been low, especially for new labor force entrants, and the share of long-term unemployed workers has moved up significantly. Workers' perceptions of job availability in the Conference Board survey have remained soft in recent months. On their own, these data would be consistent with a higher unemployment rate than currently reported. However, layoffs have moved down this year, offsetting the softness in hiring. In plain terms, workers are both less likely to find a new job and less likely to be laid off, a somewhat unusual pattern. 
Although stable, the labor market does not appear to be tight, as wage growth has slowed to a modest pace. On a 12-month basis, the wages and salaries component of the employment cost index increased 3.1 percent in September, the same pace as the change in average hourly earnings for October. Both measures have slowed noticeably from a year ago. An increasing number of workers have taken on a supplemental part-time job to make ends meet, as the share of multiple job holders has increased back to levels seen in early 2025. Given strong productivity gains in recent years, wage growth at this pace is in line with or even below the pace we would expect if inflation was running at 2 percent. 
Inflation
Progress on lowering inflation has stalled over the past two years or so. Today's consumer price index suggests that 12-month core PCE inflation likely moved up further to 3.3 percent in October, as upward pressures from higher energy prices and AI-related demand continue to flow through to core goods and services prices. 
Lack of progress on lowering inflation largely reflects a confluence of shocks unrelated to conditions in the labor market. Tariffs, energy, and AI-related price pressures each accounted for roughly one-fourth of above-target core PCE inflation over the 12 months ending in September. The remaining one-fourth likely reflects persistent effects from the inflationary shocks in recent years. Price pressures had been concentrated in a few categories, but the latest data suggest that these pressures may be broadening. 
It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations. But today's consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer. Tariff effects should further wane going forward. Energy-related price pressures should unwind when the Middle East conflict resolves. And inflation pressures related to the AI buildout seem to persist despite some early signs of slowing. I mostly view these pressures as reflecting relative price shocks in specific sectors of the economy. For example, the AI buildout has quickly shifted investment demand toward specific types of high-tech capital, putting upward pressure on prices due to relatively inelastic supply in the near term. As these shocks wane or unwind and with no inflationary pressures emerging in the labor market, my forecast is for core PCE inflation to move closer to 2 percent next year. 
Financial Conditions
Financial conditions have tightened a bit recently because of lower equity prices, higher private interest rates, and a stronger dollar. That tightening comes against a backdrop of increased market volatility. Corporate bond and mortgage rate spreads have widened, and equity valuations in the tech sector have dropped, as investors appear to be reassessing expected returns and the risks associated with increased external financing for AI investment projects. 
Economic Outlook and Risks
Looking ahead, my expectation is that policies designed to boost the economic potential of the U.S. economy would continue to support productivity, growth, and business confidence. These policies include pragmatic regulations, lower taxes, and more supportive policies toward businesses. I expect the labor market to remain stable and inflation to slow, as special factors currently holding inflation elevated gradually wane or unwind next year. Over time, I also expect increased AI adoption to raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation as lower production costs are passed through to consumer prices. 
On risks to the outlook, with the labor market improving since last year, I am more attentive to the inflation side of our mandate. Sustained supply-chain pressures from the AI buildout or greater pass-through of higher energy costs could cause inflation pressures to persist. I can also envision a scenario in which the effects of the Middle East conflict and the tech investment boom wane or unwind quickly. In this scenario, I would also expect a timelier return of core PCE inflation toward our target. 
I also see a number of risks to the outlook for economic activity, many originating in financial markets. These risks include a large correction in equity valuations, if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations, and a sharp increase in private longer-term interest rates. Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending. And higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment. I will continue to closely monitor developments in credit and equity markets to assess risks to economic growth and financial stability. 
Important Issues for Monetary Policy
I see conditions in energy markets and the AI buildout as two important issues for the economy in the months ahead. Developments in these two areas could have material effects on both sides of our mandate and could influence my views on the path for monetary policy. 
Energy Markets
The Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets, impairing the flow of oil and other commodities passing through the Strait of Hormuz, which accounted for about 20 percent of global oil supply before the conflict—roughly equivalent to total U.S. oil consumption. As tensions rose, Brent oil prices moved up to and above $110 per barrel in the second half of October before dropping sharply last week on optimism that an agreement between the U.S. and Iran could be reached following the midterm elections. Although crude oil flows in the Persian Gulf have recovered to near pre-conflict levels in recent weeks, freight rates and insurance premiums have surged because of more complex logistics and ongoing geopolitical risk, raising the cost of delivered oil to many markets around the world.

SPEECH
The science and practice of monetary policy communication: the ECB experience
Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Bank of England and its Watchers Conference
London, 10 November 2026
Monetary policy is about more than just the latest interest rate decision. It also involves communication about future economic developments and the factors shaping future policy decisions.[1] By steering the expectations of financial market participants, central bank communication shapes the full set of financial market prices across the maturity and risk spectrums, in turn affecting financing conditions and decisions around credit, saving and investment. The decisions of households and firms are also affected by their beliefs about monetary policy, which depend on how the central bank communicates.[2] 
I will divide this speech into two parts. In the first part, I will review recent contributions by ECB staff on the science of monetary policy communication.[3] In the second part, I will discuss the practice of monetary policy communication from an ECB perspective.
The science of monetary policy communication 
Greater data availability, increased computing power and artificial intelligence have substantially expanded the tools available for analysing central bank communication. Until recently, researchers relied on dictionary-based approaches to quantify the content and tone of monetary policy statements and speeches. This involved categorising specific words and expressions associated with a restrictive or accommodative stance, or with different assessments of inflation and the economic outlook.[4] Machine learning techniques and large language models (LLMs) now allow for the extensive analysis of large volumes of text in a more automated manner, taking into account the context in which words are used instead of relying solely on the frequency of individual words or predefined expressions.[5]
Recent ECB research illustrates these possibilities. A set of novel, LLM-based in-house measures of the tone of ECB monetary policy communication confirms that it becomes more hawkish during tightening phases and more dovish during easing periods. These shifts in communication closely track developments in the deposit facility rate (Chart 1, panel a).[6] The importance of communication is also illustrated by the research finding that information extracted from ECB monetary policy statements can improve forecasts of euro area core inflation several quarters ahead, even when controlling for the contributions of Eurosystem and ECB staff projections.[7]
These indicators can also be employed to test whether central bank communication follows systematic patterns that reflect the economic outlook and the policy stance. Indeed, the evidence suggests that central banks tend to communicate in a systematic manner, following “communication rules”.[8] By estimating a systematic relationship between the tone of communication on monetary policy, economic activity and inflation, ECB staff find that, in line with our primary objective of price stability, ECB communication on monetary policy systematically places more emphasis on inflation developments (Chart 1, panel b).
These new tools therefore provide valuable insights into aspects of communication that conventional financial market indicators may not fully capture. At the same time, their use requires careful validation, since the results depend on how questions are formulated and what data are used for training.[9] 
Chart 1
Evolution of ECB communication tone and “Taylor-type” communication rule weights

a) LLM-based sentiment scores and the deposit facility rate (DFR) | 
b) estimated communication rules linking tone on monetary policy with tone on inflation and economic activity

Notes: Panel a): sentiment scores across three communication dimensions (left-hand scale) and the DFR (right-hand scale). “Monetary policy” captures the tone of communication surrounding policy decisions, “economic activity” reflects assessments of economic developments and “inflation” captures signals related to price developments. A score of zero indicates a neutral tone, while positive and negative values indicate hawkish and dovish tones, respectively. Sentiment scores are calculated as moving averages of the scores for the most recent 30 texts. The sample period is 14 January 2001 to 26 October 2026. 
Panel b): regression coefficients for a model regressing the de-meaned values of the monetary policy tone on the de-meaned inflation and economic activity tones, using the tone as measured at the ECB Governing Council meeting, with the inflation and economic weights constrained to sum to one. Whiskers show 95% heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation-consistent confidence intervals. The sample period is 1 January 2001 to 13 August 2026.
Financial markets 
Financial market participants closely follow central bank communication because it provides information about both the economic and inflation outlook and the expected path of monetary policy. Both of these dimensions are relevant for asset pricing and investment decisions.
Central bank communication can influence interest rate expectations and financial conditions, independently from actual policy changes.[10] Research shows that financial analysts reassess the monetary policy stance following ECB Governing Council announcements, considering both the policy decision and the accompanying communication. Unexpected revisions in their assessment contain information beyond conventional market-based monetary policy surprises and are associated with significant effects on economic and financial conditions. For instance, even when an interest rate decision is widely anticipated and generates little immediate market reaction, the accompanying communication may lead market analysts to reassess how restrictive is monetary policy or how it is likely to evolve.[11]

Notes: Cumulated absolute high-frequency changes (with mean absolute changes in brackets) for a range of risk-free and sovereign yields across event types, computed using data from January 2004 to October 2023. The high-frequency window around the different event types is as follows: -10 minutes to +20 minutes around publication of the monetary policy press release; -10 minutes to +75 minutes around the start of the Governing Council’s press conference; -10 minutes to +50 minutes around the publication of the account of the Governing Council’s monetary policy meeting; -10 minutes to +80 minutes around the publication of the Monthly/Economic Bulletin; -10 minutes to +60 minutes around the publication of speeches other than statements to the European Parliament; and -10 minutes to +10 minutes around the publication of Bloomberg headlines. “OIS” stands for overnight index swap.
The importance of communication extends beyond Governing Council meetings. Research examining thousands of speeches, interviews, hearings and other events shows that communication in the time period between meetings can affect market interest rates across maturities. It can help markets anticipate policy changes, particularly ahead of tightening episodes, and its cumulative effect over time can be comparable to that of policy announcements, especially at longer maturities (Chart 2).[12]
Beyond shaping expectations about the future path of policy rates, communication also affects financial conditions more broadly. The tone of ECB communication can influence monetary policy uncertainty and premia on risky assets.[13] In particular, financial markets respond to several dimensions of monetary policy news: the current policy rate, the expected path of rates, and market and sovereign risk (“target”, “path”, and “risk” in Chart 3, respectively).

Average interest rate uncertainty is based on the option-implied standard deviation of the three-month Euribor one year ahead. The latest observations are for 29 October 2026.
Households and firms
Communicating with households and firms presents different challenges to communicating with markets. Unlike professional market participants, most households do not closely follow central bank communication. And even when they do encounter central bank messages, they may interpret their implications differently to market analysts. Research presented in our 2021 monetary policy strategy review suggests that information about the new inflation target reached only around one in ten consumers in the months following its announcement. Most learned about the new inflation target through television, radio and newspapers rather than directly from the ECB (Chart 4).[14]

How ECB communication reaches households

Apart from “No info”, all other options are not mutually exclusive, leading to a total sum higher than 100 per cent of the respondents. Weighted estimates. The last observation is for August 2026 (most recent Consumer Expectations Survey).
Reaching households, however, is just one part of the process. Attention to inflation varies with the economic environment. When inflation is high, households and firms tend to pay more attention, while they pay less attention when inflation is low and stable (Chart 5).[15] This matters for the transmission of monetary policy. What households and firms believe about future inflation, and how confident they are that the central bank will deliver price stability, shapes how they set wages and prices and how they adjust their spending and saving when we change interest rates.[16] 
When inflation is high, households tend to be more attentive, but they may also be less responsive to information they already know. This underscores the importance of tailoring communication to the economic environment to ensure that messages reach households when inflation is low while providing clear, relevant and informative explanations when inflation becomes more salient.[17]

Cash and the digital euro: two sides of the same coin
Introductory statement by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs of the European Parliament
Brussels, 10 November 2026
It is a pleasure to be back here for the first time since the Parliament adopted its position on the Single Currency Package, and I very much welcome the broad support it received in the plenary session on 9 July. This gives a strong democratic backing to the digital euro. Let me also thank you for the considerable work and constructive dialogue that have made this progress possible.
A swift conclusion of the ongoing trilogue negotiations would pave the way for the adoption of the Single Currency Package[1] by the end of the year as foreseen in the One Europe, One Market Roadmap.[2] This would give us the legal certainty needed to complete our preparations for the digital euro. It would also give certainty to the market regarding the planned date for a possible first issuance, which can be set only after the Regulation is adopted. A delay in adoption could instead postpone the introduction of the digital euro, further entrench Europe’s dependence on foreign providers, and make it more difficult for European companies to innovate and compete.
Europe’s achievements in payments innovation go beyond progress on the digital euro. In September we launched Pontes, which connects market distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms with the Eurosystem’s TARGET Services.[3] The launch was widely welcomed by the market, with 18 market participants and market DLT operators onboarded on day one and many others preparing to join soon. Pontes makes the settlement of tokenised transactions in central bank money an operational reality and is a major milestone in the development of digital European capital markets. On 2 November it settled the issuance of the European Stability Mechanism’s first digitally native benchmark bond of €1 billion[4], facilitating the shift in European tokenised finance from experimentation to adoption.
While I am happy to answer any questions on Pontes, I would like to focus my remarks today on the digital euro and cash.
Preparing for the digital euro pilot and first issuance 
We are moving ahead with preparations for the digital euro pilot. It will test the digital euro’s technical functionality, operational processes and user experience, using a beta version without legal tender status. 
Starting in the second half of 2027, the pilot will involve Eurosystem staff, participating payment service providers (PSPs) and selected merchants offering everyday services – for example in canteens – at the ECB and participating national central banks.
We have seen strong market interest in the pilot and, in July, we announced the 36 PSPs selected to join the pilot from more than 50 applicants.[5] They include banks and non-bank providers, and cover a broad range of business models, sizes and geographical locations.
We are working closely with participating PSPs to hear their views and benefit from their experience.[6] 
In September we opened an additional call for online and mobile merchants to join the pilot to test remote payments. The final selection of merchants will be announced early next year.[7] 
This collaboration with market players is essential. The digital euro must work on a technical level, but also in everyday life – for consumers, merchants and PSPs.
Looking further ahead, we are planning for the digital euro rollout. 
On our side, we plan to ensure that all relevant use cases[8] for the digital euro are made technically available from first issuance. At the same time, feedback from market participants[9] shows that a gradual rollout would support a smooth and successful first issuance by giving them sufficient time to adapt. We are glad that the co-legislators intend to provide legal clarity on the feasibility of such a phased rollout in shops. 
In preparation for first issuance, we are also working more closely with the market on the digital euro innovation platform. 
In September we launched a new call for expression of interest, inviting private companies and organisations to explore how the digital euro can foster market innovation.[10] The next wave of activities, including testing conditional payments and exploring applications of artificial intelligence in payments, will run from January to June 2027.[11]
Redesigning euro banknotes 
Innovation also extends to banknotes. In July we invited Europeans to share their views on ten shortlisted design proposals for the new euro banknotes based on the themes “European culture” and “Rivers and birds”. 
The survey received almost 10 million responses, with high participation across all euro area countries and age groups.[12] This demonstrates how deeply Europeans care about their money.
The survey results will inform the ECB Governing Council’s decision on the final design concept, expected around the end of this year. At that point, we will also publish the survey results. First denominations of the new banknote series are expected to enter into circulation in the early 2030s.[13]
But cash must also remain widely available and accepted in practice. We therefore support strong legislative provisions on mandatory cash acceptance, access to cash across the euro area and the resilience of cash infrastructure.
Conclusion 
Let me conclude.
In today’s uncertain geopolitical environment, timely progress on the digital euro is essential to strengthen Europe’s autonomy in payments. We are doing our part by progressing with the technical preparations. But the adoption of the legal framework is necessary to finalise the digital euro’s design and Rulebook[14] and, ultimately, to issue the digital euro.
In two months’ time we will mark the 25th anniversary of euro banknotes and coins entering circulation. While cash is still widely used in shops, digital payments are growing. I therefore hope that by then we will have a strong legal framework in place: one that both safeguards the acceptance of cash and gives Europeans a digital form of cash alongside it.
Thank you.

Tokyo
and Midland, Texas – November 9, 2026 – Rakuten Group, Inc. and AST SpaceMobile, Inc. (NASDAQ: ASTS), the company
building the first and only space-based cellular broadband network accessible directly by everyday smartphones, agreed to establish Rakuten
AST, Inc. on November 6, 2026 (Japan Standard Time)*1. The joint venture is tasked with building a direct-to-device communications
network in Japan using low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites to provide service to commercially available smartphones, strengthening Japan’s
communications infrastructure in the event of disasters and other emergencies.
The
Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications’ (MIC) selected the joint proposal from Rakuten’s preparatory company and
Rakuten Mobile, Inc. for the publicly solicited “J-LEO: Japan Low Earth Orbit Satellite Communications Project”*2.
Rakuten AST is expected to receive up to 148 billion yen (approx. 1 billion USD) in support over approximately three years under
J-LEO, through the Communications and Information Network Association of Japan (CIAJ), the organization established to manage the fund*3,4.
Through this joint venture, Rakuten AST will collaborate with AST SpaceMobile to deploy and manage satellites compatible with mid-band
spectrum, in order to establish a satellite communications network and commence domestic operations by the end of March 2029.
 | 
The
J-LEO Project will leverage the largest communication satellites ever deployed in LEO to build domestic communications infrastructure
that enables direct satellite-to-smartphone connectivity and strengthens economic security. In addition to extending cellular broadband
connectivity to areas with limited or no terrestrial coverage, the project aims to ensure cellular broadband connectivity during emergencies,
such as natural disasters, by establishing a framework for emergency inter-carrier roaming among mobile network operators.
Through
Rakuten AST, Rakuten and Rakuten Mobile aim to establish a non-terrestrial network (NTN) managed and operated in Japan. The companies
will deploy and operate a resilient, stable communications infrastructure capable of maintaining priority and stable connectivity, independent
of external conditions – even in times of emergency.
The
satellite communications service to be deployed by Rakuten AST will leverage AST SpaceMobile’s large-scale satellites to enable
high-speed internet connectivity — such as video streaming and social media — on off-the-shelf smartphones without the need
for specialized equipment*5. Because the base station equipment is installed on ground-based infrastructure, Japanese telecommunications
operators can flexibly and autonomously manage and operate the network.
AST
SpaceMobile will supply the satellites to power Japan’s sovereign D2D constellation. Beyond priority Japanese domestic market usage,
Rakuten AST also plans to work with AST SpaceMobile to provide these services through AST SpaceMobile to its customers worldwide, subject
to regulatory approval.
Rakuten
Mobile will also work with AST SpaceMobile to advance the use of AI edge computing and plans to develop AI-driven spectrum management
technology, exploring their application for higher-speed data communications and industry-specific solutions such as IoT. The company
aims to expand its solution offerings beyond telecommunications carriers to include connectivity-reliant industries, such as logistics,
infrastructure monitoring, construction, and agriculture.
Mickey
Mikitani, Chairman and CEO, Rakuten Group, commented, “This project is a key pillar of Rakuten Mobile’s network strategy.
By building an integrated framework spanning satellite procurement through operations and accelerating technological innovation, we will
contribute to the development of disaster-resilient communications infrastructure and the improvement of Japan’s communications
environment. We will maximize capital efficiency and pursue the expansion of business opportunities in the satellite communications sector.”
Abel
Avellan, Founder, Chairman and CEO, AST SpaceMobile, commented, “This represents a significant milestone for AST SpaceMobile
and validates the importance of space-based cellular broadband connectivity as countries around the world increasingly recognize the
technology as a critical complement to terrestrial wireless infrastructure to realize the goal of 100% broadband availability wherever
people work, live and travel. Through our technology, we will enhance the resilience of Japan’s communications infrastructure while
strengthening our global network by leveraging capacity that can also be utilized outside of Japan.”
 | 
In
addition to this project, Rakuten Mobile plans to begin commercial-environment testing of its satellite-to-mobile service within 2026,
under the strategic partnership between Rakuten and AST SpaceMobile established in March 2020*6.
Rakuten,
Rakuten Mobile, and AST SpaceMobile will continue working toward the early realization of D2D satellite communications, advancing the
development of resilient communications networks.

The Economic Outlook and Some Thoughts on Labor Market Dynamism 
 Governor Christopher J. Waller 
At the Bank of England Watchers Conference King’s Business School and Money, Macro and Finance Society, London, United Kingdom 
 Share 
 Watch Live 
Thank you, Paul, and welcome to Bank of England watchers, who I suspect are watching the Federal Reserve as well.1 
My subject today is the outlook for the U.S. economy and the implications for monetary policy. I think there is little disagreement about the basics of that outlook. The U.S. economy is growing strongly, with a labor market that has brought employment close to its long-term rate. But inflation remains too high, so I will explain why I believe further tightening of monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach 2 percent in the medium term. 
The outline of my speech is to first explain why I voted to hold the policy rate steady at the most recent meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Then I will talk about the general state of the U.S. economy. After that, I will ask some open-ended questions about the dynamism of the U.S. labor market that are important to consider over the longer run. I'll follow that by a discussion of recent inflation data and then describe my views about the future path of monetary policy. 
At our most recent meeting, I supported the FOMC majority in holding monetary policy at its current setting. As I said in a speech a couple weeks before then, my rationale was that the Committee's communication about the likely tightening of policy had already led financial markets to price in some tightening.2 When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out—it is not necessary, for example, to raise rates at consecutive meetings. 
If, however, the hikes are not carried out, markets will reduce expectations of rate hikes and rates will immediately fall, which would loosen monetary policy in an undesirable way. So, while the precise timing of the hikes doesn't matter, ensuring that the promised hikes are implemented in a reasonable period of time does. 
Let me turn to the economy. Economic output continues to grow at a healthy pace. The initial estimate was that real gross domestic product (GDP) rose 3.4 percent in the third quarter, supported by strong consumer spending and robust investment. Consumption growth was helped by a booming stock market, and investment by businesses continued to surge, especially in high-tech equipment associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout. I expect GDP growth is backing off a bit in the current quarter, as consumer spending slows to levels that I think are more consistent with household income and wealth, but output will continue to grow at a solid pace. 
The labor market has also been solid. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent in October, the same rate it was over the summer. Job creation, which has been fluctuating widely month to month for some time, saw October gains of 165,000 jobs and 85,000 jobs added to estimates of the previous two months. To look through the volatility, the 6-month and 12-month average payroll gains have been closer to 80,000 jobs a month. This level is a bit above most estimates of the breakeven level needed to keep the unemployment rate steady but entirely consistent with my view that the supply and demand for labor are in rough balance. 
While the labor market has been stable, for over a year now it has been what is best characterized as "low hire, low fire." One can understand this characterization by looking at job separation and hiring rates today and comparing them with what they were before the pandemic (see figures 1 and 2). You will see that the rate of separations, the sum of layoffs and quits, has been persistently low the past few years compared with a decade ago. The hiring rate is also low. This is unusual because, in a strong labor market, the hiring rate is usually high. Hiring tends to be low when the labor market is weak, which is when the firing rate is often elevated. What is unusual today, and may be unprecedented, is the extent to which both firing and hiring are now so low. 
These data have led me to consider a question that has longer-term implications for the economy and monetary policy: Does a stable labor market necessarily mean it's a healthy labor market? To illustrate the difference, if your mom was in the hospital and the doctor told you her condition was stable, you would be relieved but you wouldn't say she is healthy. I am concerned that the low hire, low fire equilibrium in the labor market means it has lost some of its dynamism, which is important for productivity growth and real wages. If the labor market is in fact showing less dynamism, is it an issue for monetary policy? While I don't have answers to these questions, I do think the questions are worth asking. 
This discussion starts with distinguishing between net employment growth and gross flows in and out of employment. Behind the monthly job creation numbers that get most of the world's attention is the enormous churn in the labor market. For example, the 60,000 jobs created in September was a net change in the level of employment, but it is dwarfed by the more than 5 million people who left their jobs that month and the more than 5 million who were hired. Despite the low separation and hiring rates, the level of separations and hiring is huge. When I was a professor, I would use the following analogy for my students. If you stand by a river, you can measure the water level. If you return the next day and measure again, you will likely find that the water level is unchanged—it is stable. But in fact, a massive amount of water has flowed downstream since the day before. The same goes for the labor market—there is a lot of churning even if the level of employment is stable. 
The question is, does churn in the labor market matter? If so, is labor market churn bad or good? One could argue that this churn is inefficient. Why are people and firms wasting time swapping workers across jobs? If workers simply stayed at their firms, and firms never let them go, employment would be stable and resources would be saved from putting workers into new jobs. But would it mean the labor market is healthy? 
The answer is that the churn in hiring and firing is actually good for the economy. This churn reflects a dynamic market that allows labor resources to be allocated to more productive uses. If a worker and firm are not in a good, productive match, then it is more efficient and better for the economy for the worker and firm to separate and look for new partners. When more productive matches are formed, productivity, real wages, and profits will be higher. In this situation, employment may not be stable, but it is healthier. 
I believe this churn is what leads to the exceptional performance of the U.S. economy. The relative ease of starting businesses in the United States, compared with many other advanced economies, is a big advantage. The relative ease of firing employees, compared with many European Union economies, is surely not welcome by the workers affected, but cumulatively it was a factor that drove the stronger recovery in the United States from the pandemic recession. This flexibility in hiring and firing promotes a better match between skills of the worker and those demanded by businesses, making the most productive use of their abilities. As a result, this churn boosts the capacity of the economy and allows incomes to grow without inflationary pressure. 
So, given this discussion, how do we interpret the current low hire, low fire economy? Does it indicate that the U.S. labor market has become less dynamic and less healthy, which has implications for the economic outlook and for monetary policy? I will first consider the possible causes of this lower dynamism and then the possible implications. 
One explanation for the lower dynamism is that some of the decline in both hiring and firing may reflect, in part, a continuation of longer-run trends that were in place even before the pandemic. First, it is well known that the workforce is aging for a number of reasons: People are living longer and are healthier and more active at older ages; many members of the large post–World War II baby boom are in their 60s and 70s; and birth rates have declined, which increases the relative age of the workforce. This aging affects the dynamism of the labor market because older workers switch jobs less frequently, since many have managed over time to find better job matches and because older workers are less likely to relocate for work. The second trend is that the level of education of the workforce is increasing over time. More educated workers experience less job churn in general and, during downturns, face lower rates of job separations. Since 2010, the share of adults 25 and older with at least a bachelor's degree has increased from 28 percent to 37 percent.3 
If these were the only reasons for the decline in labor market dynamism, then it would be at a level consistent with these trend factors, suggesting an appropriate degree of dynamism with no implications for monetary policy. But the data suggest that, even after accounting for these factors, labor market dynamism still seems somewhat low. There are several possible reasons. 
One is that hiring and job-switching may have been restrained by the confluence of factors that have raised economic uncertainty since early 2025: the advent of AI, tariffs, changes in immigration policy and enforcement, and a general level of uncertainty about the economic outlook that has made business planning particularly challenging. One piece of evidence was a special question posed in the Federal Reserve's November 2025 Beige Book survey of economic conditions: Employers reported in November 2025 that hiring was unusually restrained because of uncertainty. I don't think uncertainty has diminished much since then. And another piece of evidence is in the most recent Beige Book, showing that several Fed Districts reported firms had delayed hiring or anticipate less job creation after investing in AI.

GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026
Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the advance estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent.
The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. For more information, refer to the "Technical Notes" below.
Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 4.9 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 4.6 percent in the second quarter.
The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 3.0 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 5.6 percent in the second quarter. Technical Notes
Sources of change for real GDP
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent (0.8 percent at a quarterly rate 1) in the third quarter, reflecting increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased.
More information on the source data and BEA assumptions that underlie the third-quarter estimate is shown in the key source data and assumptions table.
The increase in investment primarily reflected increases in private inventory investment and in equipment.
The largest contributors to the increase in private inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing (both led by nondurable goods industries), based primarily on Census Bureau inventory book value data.
Within equipment, the increase was led by information processing equipment (mainly computers and peripheral equipment), based primarily on data for imports from the U.S. Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services report and the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September.
The increase in consumer spending reflected increases in both services and goods.
Within services, the increase was led by health care (mainly hospitals and outpatient services), based primarily on U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Current Employment Statistics, and food services and accommodations (mainly purchased meals and beverages), based on Census Bureau Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS) data.
Within goods, the increase was led by other nondurable goods (mainly prescription drugs), based on Census Bureau MRTS data.
Within government spending, the increase was more than accounted for by federal government spending, led by nondefense consumption expenditures. The pattern of nondefense spending primarily reflected sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, based on data from the U.S. Department of Energy. Within the National Economic Accounts, sales are deducted from government consumption expenditures. In the third quarter, sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve were less than sales in the second quarter, resulting in an increase in consumption expenditures. Because the oil sold by the government is reflected as an increase in other components of GDP, there is no direct effect on GDP.
Exports and imports primarily reflected Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services data as well as the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September. The decrease in exports primarily reflected a decrease in goods (led by petroleum and related products). The largest contributor to imports was capital goods, except automotive.

U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela in July were highest since 2017 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly 
In July 2026, U.S. imports of crude oil from Venezuela averaged 701,000 barrels per day (b/d), the most since May 2017, before decreasing to 655,000 b/d in August, according to data published in our Petroleum Supply Monthly. 
Crude oil imports from Venezuela started the year at 200,000 b/d and have steadily increased most months this year. Increased imports from Venezuela are supported by high crude oil demand from U.S. refineries because of high global refinery margins and the easing of U.S. government restrictions on purchases from the country. Many refineries on the U.S. Gulf Coast (PADD 3) are configured to process heavy sour crude oil grades, such as those from Venezuela. 
According to data from Vortexa, the majority of crude oil exports from Venezuela in 2025 were destined for China. In 2026, Venezuela has exported no crude oil to China, and the United States has instead been the largest single destination by volume for Venezuelan crude oil exports. 
U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela stopped shortly after the United States imposed sanctions on state oil company Petróleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA) in January 2019. In November 2022, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control granted Chevron waivers to resume exporting crude oil from its joint venture operations in Venezuela to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries; Chevron resumed these exports in January 2023. 
The U.S. government eased restrictions on PDVSA following the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January 2026 and took additional measures to authorize U.S. companies to invest in the country to increase Venezuelan domestic crude oil production.

 November 5, 2026 
Refineries have shifted production away from gasoline to middle distillates 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly 
Particularly high refinery margins for distillate fuel oil and jet fuel have contributed to shifts in the refinery yields of major products in 2026. Data from our latest Petroleum Supply Monthly—which includes data through August 2026—indicate refinery yields of gasoline have decreased significantly this year to support increased production of distillate fuel oil and jet fuel, sometimes referred to as middle distillates due to their relative cut points in the oil refining process. 
Petroleum refinery yields represent the share of a specific fuel that is produced from each barrel of crude oil a given refinery (or group of refineries) processes. The U.S. refining fleet tends to have a strong refinery yield of gasoline—typically between 45%–50%. In general terms, for every 100 barrels of crude oil U.S. refiners process, they produce about 45–50 barrels of gasoline. Typically, the most important refinery yields in the United States are the refinery yields of motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil (often sold as diesel fuel), and kerosene-type jet fuel. The combined yield of motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and jet fuel typically accounts for between 85%–90% of the petroleum products produced by the U.S. refining fleet. 
Despite high gasoline prices, refinery yields of motor gasoline have trended below the five-year (2021–2025) low throughout 2026. This decline largely reflects refinery efforts to shift as much of their yields as possible into the production of distillate fuel oil and jet fuel, where margins are significantly higher because of constrained global supplies for these fuels. From January through August 2026, refinery yields of gasoline have averaged less than 45% and have been well below the five-year low in every month. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly 
Conversely, yields of distillate fuel oil have generally been higher than last year and have been above the five-year average in every month. Even more than for gasoline, crack spreads and refinery margins for distillate fuel have been elevated for most of this year in response to limits on global supplies of the fuel. 
Refinery yields of jet fuel have also been relatively high this year. The U.S. refinery fleet exceeded an average jet fuel yield of 12% for the first time in March 2026, according to EIA data. Since then, the fleetwide average jet fuel yield has remained at or above 12% through the latest Petroleum Supply Monthly data for August 2026. Jet fuel yields were already setting the five-year high for most of 2025; elevated jet fuel margins in 2026 have provided a persistent incentive for refiners to continue maximizing jet fuel production. 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly

 November 3, 2026 
Global refinery inputs fell sharply in the second quarter of 2026 before modest recovery 
Data source: Kpler
Note: 2Q2025=second quarter of 2025 
Global crude oil refinery inputs fell by 4.8 million barrels per day (b/d) in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), or 6%, following the start of conflict in late February in the Middle East, according to data from Kpler. Throughput then increased by 1.8 million b/d in the third quarter, primarily as refiners in the region adjusted to new trade flows. 
Crude oil inputs to refineries typically increase in the second and third quarters of the year as refiners complete planned maintenance and gear up to meet peak seasonal demand for refined products, such as gasoline and jet fuel. Global crude oil inputs increased by 0.3 million b/d in the second quarter of 2025 and by another 2 million b/d in the third quarter. 
The countries with the largest refining capacity in the world are the United States, China, Russia, and India. Refining in countries most directly impacted by the loss of crude oil supply from conflict in the Strait of Hormuz saw the largest declines. Crude oil refinery inputs in China fell by 2.1 million b/d in 2Q26 and by an additional 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26, while crude oil inputs in India, South Korea, and Japan fell by more than 1.0 million b/d collectively in 2Q26 before rebounding by 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26. 
Crude oil inputs also fell in the Middle East as the closure of the strait significantly limited the export of refined products. Crude oil inputs fell by 0.7 million b/d in Kuwait, 0.7 million b/d in the United Arab Emirates, 0.3 million b/d in Saudi Arabia, and 0.2 million b/d in Iran in 2Q26. Total crude oil inputs in these four countries increased by 0.4 million b/d in 3Q26. 
Increased attacks on Russian oil infrastructure during the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine reduced refinery crude oil inputs in Russia by 0.6 million b/d in 2Q26 and an additional 0.8 million b/d in 3Q26. Russia is a major fuel exporter, especially of diesel fuel, so the decline in exports affected global diesel markets that were already tight from earlier geopolitical developments. This loss in refinery operations compounded reduced refining activity in Asia and the Middle East, contributing to diesel prices increasing to the highest nominal levels on record in September. 
Although crude oil inputs were falling in some countries in the second and third quarters of 2026, they increased in the United States and in some other regions that were able to find alternative sources of supply. Crude oil refinery inputs in the United States increased by 0.5 million b/d in 2Q26 and by an additional 0.5 million b/d in 3Q26, as the United States increasingly exported refined products around the world to make up for lost supply. 
Global refinery crude oil inputs recovered somewhat in 3Q26, increasing by 1.8 million b/d overall as increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz, alternative routes, and ship-to-ship transfers put more Middle Eastern crude oil on the global market. Despite the increase in oil flows and refinery inputs, crude oil inputs in 3Q26 still remained about 5% lower on average than during the same period of 2025.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S. population. It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers. Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals. Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U). 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
weeks during the previous 12 months. The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living. Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments). All taxes directly associated with the
purchase and use of items are included in the index. Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
all 75 locations. Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
geographic areas and every other month in other areas. Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.
In calculating the index, price changes for the various items in each location are aggregated using weights, which
represent their importance in the spending of the appropriate population group. Local data are then combined to obtain
a U.S. city average. For the CPI-U and CPI-W, separate indexes are also published by size of city, by region of the
country, for cross-classifications of regions and population-size classes, and for 23 selected local areas. Area
indexes do not measure differences in the level of prices among cities; they only measure the average change in prices
for each area since the base period. For the C-CPI-U, data are issued only at the national level. The CPI-U and CPI-W
are considered final when released, but the C-CPI-U is issued in preliminary form and subject to three subsequent
quarterly revisions.

 THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - OCTOBER 2026 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed 
little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in 
professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. 
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures labor 
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment survey 
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information about the 
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note. 
Household Survey Data 
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, 
changed little in October. The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to 
4.3 percent since March. (See table A-1.) 
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for 
adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent), teenagers (13.9 percent), and people who are 
White (3.7 percent), Black (6.6 percent), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent). (See 
tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.) 
The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed 
little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed 
people. (See table A-12.) 
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 
59.3 percent, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January. 
(See table A-1.) 
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in 
October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time 
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. (See table A-8.) 
In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at 
6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively 
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. (See 
table A-1.) 
Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to 
the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were 
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for 
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the 
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over 
the month at 448,000. (See Summary table A.) 
Establishment Survey Data 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, higher than the average monthly gain 
of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business 
services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. (See table B-1.) 
Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the 
average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend 
up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and 
waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises 
(+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 
2025. 
Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the 
prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care 
services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000). 
In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and 
messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 
104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) 
contributing most of the gain. 
Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 
since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic 
product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing 
(+4,000). 
Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, 
quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; 
financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government. 
In October, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 
cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00. Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased 
by 3.1 percent. In October, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and nonsupervisory 
employees rose by 12 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $32.75. (See tables B-3 and B-8.) 
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in 
October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up 
by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on 
private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours. (See tables B-2 and B-7.) 
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 
to +186,000, and the change for September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With 
these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. (Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government 
agencies since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.)

 PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - SEPTEMBER 2026
The Producer Price Index for final demand increased 1.3 percent in September, seasonally 
adjusted, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Final demand prices moved up 0.5 
percent in August and 0.2 percent in July. (See table A.) The September increase is the largest 
advance since rising 1.7 percent in March 2022. On an unadjusted basis, the index for final 
demand climbed 6.3 percent for the 12 months ended in September, the largest 12-month 
increase since moving up 6.4 percent in December 2022.
In September, prices for final demand goods rose 2.6 percent, and the index for final demand 
services advanced 0.8 percent.
Prices for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services moved up 0.5 percent in September 
after increasing 0.3 percent in August. For the 12 months ended in September, the index for final 
demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 5.0 percent.
Final Demand
Final demand goods: Prices for final demand goods advanced 2.6 percent in September, the largest 
increase since data were first calculated in December 2009. Over 80 percent of the broad-based rise 
in September is attributable to the index for final demand energy, which jumped 10.8 percent. Prices 
for final demand foods and for final demand goods less foods and energy advanced 1.2 percent and 
0.3 percent, respectively.
Product detail: Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to 
prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3 percent. The indexes for diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, 
jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose. In contrast, prices for chicken eggs 
dropped 39.7 percent. The indexes for thermoplastic resins and materials and for commercial electric 
power also declined. (See table 2.)
Final demand services: Prices for final demand services moved up 0.8 percent in September, the 
largest rise since advancing 0.8 percent in April. Nearly half of the broad-based September increase 
can be attributed to a 1.4-percent rise in margins for final demand trade services. The indexes for 
final demand transportation and warehousing services and for final demand services less trade, 
transportation, and warehousing also advanced, 3.4 percent and 0.3 percent, respectively.
Product detail: Over 20 percent of the September increase in prices for final demand services can be 
traced to margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling, which advanced 3.9 percent. The indexes 
for truck transportation of freight, food and alcohol wholesaling, traveler accommodation services, 
food retailing, and airline passenger services also rose. Conversely, margins for automotive fuels and 
lubricants retailing dropped 30.3 percent. The indexes for securities brokerage, dealing, and 
investment advice and for chemicals and allied products wholesaling also fell.

goods rising 2.5 percent, prices for unprocessed goods moving up 8.4 percent, and the index for services 
advancing 0.9 percent. (See tables B and C.)
Processed goods for intermediate demand: The index for processed goods for intermediate demand 
moved up 2.5 percent in September, the largest rise since jumping 2.8 percent in May. Over 80 percent of 
the September advance is attributable to a 10.2-percent increase in prices for processed energy goods. The 
indexes for processed materials less foods and energy and for processed foods and feeds also moved up, 
0.5 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively. For the 12 months ended in September, prices for processed 
goods for intermediate demand rose 14.1 percent, the largest 12-month increase since advancing 14.3 
percent in August 2022.
Product detail: Nearly half of the September rise in the index for processed goods for intermediate 
demand can be traced to a 21.0-percent increase in prices for diesel fuel. The indexes for gasoline, jet 
fuel, lubricating oil base stocks, prepared animal feeds, and fabricated structural metal products also 
moved higher. In contrast, prices for commercial electric power declined 0.6 percent. The indexes for 
thermoplastic resins and materials and for dry sausage also fell.
Unprocessed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for unprocessed goods for intermediate demand 
moved up 8.4 percent in September, the largest increase since rising 9.2 percent in February 2022. Over 
80 percent of the September advance is attributable to the index for unprocessed energy materials, which 
jumped 22.2 percent. Prices for unprocessed nonfood materials less energy and for unprocessed foodstuffs 
and feedstuffs also moved up, 2.5 percent and 0.8 percent, respectively. For the 12 months ended in 
September, the index for unprocessed goods for intermediate demand rose 21.5 percent, the largest 12-
month increase since advancing 29.2 percent in September 2022.
Product detail: Leading the September increase in prices for unprocessed goods for intermediate demand, 
the index for crude petroleum jumped 28.3 percent. Prices for grains; hay, hayseeds, and oilseeds; natural 
gas; fresh and dry vegetables; and nonferrous metal ores also rose. Conversely, the index for raw milk 
decreased 12.3 percent. Prices for slaughter chickens and for aluminum base scrap also declined.

REAL EARNINGS  OCTOBER 2026 
All employees 
Real average hourly earnings for all employees were unchanged from September to October, seasonally 
adjusted, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. This result stems from an increase of 0.4 
percent in average hourly earnings combined with an increase of 0.4 percent in the Consumer Price 
Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U). 
Real average weekly earnings were unchanged over the month due to no change in real average hourly 
earnings combined with no change in the average workweek. 
******************************************************************************************************** 
* Federal Government Shutdown * 
* * 
* This release usually includes an over-the-year analysis of changes to real earnings. BLS could not * 
* collect the relevant Consumer Price Index data for the October 2025 reference period due to a lapse * 
* in apprpriations in late 2025. For that reason, over-the-year comparisons from October 2025 to * 
* October 2026 are not available. * 
* * 
******************************************************************************************************** 
Production and nonsupervisory employees 
Real average hourly earnings for production and nonsupervisory employees increased 0.1 percent from 
September to October, seasonally adjusted. This result stems from a 0.4-percent increase in average 
hourly earnings combined with an increase of 0.3 percent in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage 
Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). 
Real average weekly earnings decreased 0.3 percent over the month due to the change in real average 
hourly earnings combined with a decrease of 0.3 percent in the average workweek. 
___________
